mechanism: The cued base's T 0.6 loops are seeded by near-repeats piling up in its own earlier text: each partly repeated block (case lists, re-derivations, table rows) raises the probability of the next repeat, so the loop hazard at a position depends on how self-similar (compressible) the text written so far is, not on position, per-token surprise or problem difficulty; the base finishes from RL's prefix because RL's text is less self-similar, not because it is mathematically sounder.
starts_from: knowledge-1497e8 (base finishes 48/78 from RL's prefix vs 23/78 from its own, at similar prefix lengths), with knowledge-787e53 (base loops have periods of hundreds of characters) and result-dadeec
differs_from: r3-revise-2 puts loop onset at impasse positions whose timing depends on the sampler; r2-all-2 and r2-surprises-1 use per-token surprise; r1-across-1 blames induction circuitry that RL weakens; r3-across-2 uses tail-token escape. This one says the hazard is a dose-response on block-level self-similarity of the history, so two prefixes with equal mean log-prob but different compressibility differ in loop rate. m02 is about length as a correctness signal at T 1.0, not about loops.
first_test: On r3 base-01 F_math500 (T 0.6 cue, rln3 rows): for every answer compute the zlib ratio of the text before min(1,500 tokens, rule-A onset) and fit cap_hit on it with mean_logprob of the same span and the RL-length quartile (from T2 n_generated) as covariates. Then on K_own and K_rl compute the same ratio of the prefix and fit 'finished' on ratio plus prefix_kind. Refuted if the within-quartile AUROC of the ratio is below 0.65, or if prefix_kind is still significant and the ratio is not once both are in the K model.

mechanism: When the cued base goes down a wrong line it writes abandoned attempts and restarts that add tokens before it settles, so within one problem a base sample's length is a direct readout of how many attempts failed; RL's added tokens are habitual verification written on right and wrong answers alike, which removes that within-problem signal.
starts_from: result-cbe0bc (breaking vote ties by the shortest finished sample fixes 7 and breaks 0 for the base, but does nothing for RL, where the longest-sample control is as good), with result-5e17a6 (263 base answers <= 2,000 tokens, 13 wrong)
differs_from: No graveyard entry uses within-problem length. r1-across-2 and r1-all-1 relate length to budget and degradation across problems; r3-surprises-1 is about tail slips. m06 is about whether RL re-checks conditionally on a candidate being wrong, read from text; m02 is a claim about the base's sample-length distribution within a problem and is testable from lengths and grades alone.
first_test: day1_3 math500_base_cue-01 and math500_rl-01 rows.jsonl (attempt 0, finished samples only): for each problem with at least one right and one wrong sample, the within-problem Spearman correlation of n_new with score_v3. Refuted if the base's mean correlation is above -0.3, or if RL's mean correlation is within 0.15 of the base's (both models carry the same length signal).

mechanism: On-policy RL converges to the change nearest the base in KL that raises reward, and on math text the nearest such change is the same for the Math and Code rewards, so the two nearly orthogonal weight differences make the base solve the same problems (they flip the same items), while differing in style such as length.
starts_from: result-c9b27e and result-4b0d5f (Math and Code deltas cos 0.014, sign agreement 50.8 %, yet Code-RL cue 450 vs RL cue 457 on MATH-500 and Code 187 = theta(0.5) 190 on hard328, with Code using about 30 % fewer tokens)
differs_from: r2-all-1 and r2-revise-1 predicted that Code-RL gives no math gain because of sign disagreement (refuted by Code 390/450). r3-across-1, r3-surprises-2 and r3-revise-1 split the gain into a shared part and a math-specific part by dose and difficulty. This one makes no claim about dose; it says the item-level effect is shared, which is an item-agreement claim. It conflicts with m09 (Code fixes only failures at the ending), and the per-class split in m09's test separates the two.
first_test: Per-problem 0/1 on MATH-500 for code_cue (0203), rl_cue (e985), theta0.5_cue (683b), random_cue (6429) and base T1; on hard328 for Code a619, theta a5f4/34ad, RL 86ef. Compute Cohen's kappa of Code vs RL-cue and of Code vs theta0.5, and as a ceiling the mean kappa between pairs of RL samples in day1_3 math500_rl-01 (same-model resampling). Refuted if kappa(Code, RL cue) is under 0.7 of the RL-RL ceiling, or no higher than kappa(Code, random cell) after matching accuracies.

mechanism: A partial weight difference base + a(RL - base) does not produce an intermediate policy; it produces a per-sample mixture of two discrete modes, the base's ('Answer:' line, short, few 'Wait') and RL's (boxed, long, many 'Wait'). The dose a sets the probability that a sample enters RL's mode, early in generation, and each mode then scores like its endpoint on that problem.
starts_from: result-4b0d5f (plain row 224/405/443/463 at a = 0/0.25/0.5/1, cue row nearly flat from 0.25) and knowledge-69adda (every recovering arm takes RL's format and length)
differs_from: r1-all-2 said any unbiased fraction of the delta flips one saturating switch fully, so at small a nearly all samples are RL-like; r3-external-2 and r3-revise-1 describe components that grow with dose inside every sample; r2-across-1 has the partial delta graded in fork entropy. Here, at a = 0.25 plain, about three quarters of samples are fully RL-like and a quarter fully base-like, with no intermediate answers. m03 compares Code with Math at the item level; m04 is about the distribution of single answers within one theta cell.
first_test: On theta0.25_plain (ffca), theta0.5_plain (8118) and theta0.25_cue (b029), compute per answer: final format (mode_v3 boxed vs 'Answer:'), 'Wait'/'Hmm' per 1k tokens, and log n_new. Fit a 2-class classifier on base T3/T1 vs RL T2 answers and score the theta answers. Refuted if fewer than 80 % of theta answers get a class posterior above 0.9, or if the distribution of Wait rates in theta0.25_plain is unimodal and centred between the endpoints (dip test p > 0.1), or if the RL-like share at theta0.25 plain is outside 0.6-0.9.

mechanism: Each problem's text sets how strongly the base's prior favours its exam-answer register over its reasoning-trace register. The three-token cue overrides that prior only where it is weak, and RL's per-layer push (whose late readouts carry the cue token) overrides it everywhere. So the residual cue-vs-RL gap sits on the problems where the base found the cue least likely.
starts_from: knowledge-0b450e (the base opens '.\n\nOkay' by itself on 168/500 problems), result-e2482e (cue token in the top 15 of 13/96 late RL-delta readouts) and result-54f212 (one constant vector per layer closes 23-31 % of KL)
differs_from: r1-all-2, r1-surprises-1 and r3-revise-1 treat the cue as reproducing a deliberative mode exactly or at saturation everywhere; r3-across-1 locates the residual by base p and difficulty. This one predicts a per-problem quantity, the cue's log-prob under the base, that should predict the residual gap independently of difficulty. m08 explains the item pattern by pretraining exposure and m07 by the structure of wrong answers, not by register prior.
first_test: Join rln5 map-01 checks.json (T1 list, cue_logprob_base per problem) to t1_t2_items per_problem.json (cell, t2_generated_tokens). Within RL-length quartiles, compute the AUROC of -cue_logprob_base for rl_only vs both. Also check whether it predicts a final 'Answer:' line in T1.jsonl. Refuted if the pooled within-quartile AUROC is below 0.6, or if T3 (plain base) problems that spontaneously open with '.\n\nOkay' show the same rl_only rate as the rest.

mechanism: RL lowered the wrap-up prior uniformly (hold-on up, 'So'/'Answer'/EOS down in the lens readout at every position). It did not install an error detector. So RL re-checks a right intermediate answer as often as a wrong one, and the accuracy gain comes only because a re-check costs little when the answer is right and changes the answer when it is wrong.
starts_from: result-b4c576 and result-cb82cf (hold-on +1.08 pts, wrap-up -1.40 pts, a general habit not larger on the 65 RL-only problems), result-c4411d (after a wrong result, hold-on rises nearly equally in both models) and result-fdc8da (RL's P(stop) < 0.5 at 16.5 % of the base's true ends)
differs_from: r2-revise-2 (and the d' finding it imported) says RL is a better error detector, with re-checks far more frequent after wrong candidates. Here the re-check rate does not depend on correctness. r1-across-2 and r3-all-1 frame the checking as budget control or math-specific checking learned from truncation. m02 makes claims about lengths; m06 makes claims about where in RL's text re-checks follow candidates.
first_test: In T2.jsonl (RL) and T1.jsonl (base) texts, extract every intermediate candidate answer (a boxed value, 'the answer is', or a final '= value' line before the end), grade each candidate with grader/rln4_grader_v3.py against gold, and mark whether a hold-on word ('Wait', 'let me check', 'verify', 'Hmm') follows within 200 tokens. Refuted if RL's re-check rate after wrong candidates is at least 1.5x its rate after right candidates.

mechanism: The base's wrong answers come in two kinds: problem-specific attractors (one wrong value that most samples of both models reach, from a shared misreading inherited from pretraining) and scattered slips. RL concentrates probability on the base's own paths, so it removes the scattered errors and keeps the attractors. RL's wrong answers therefore mostly equal the base's modal wrong answer, and RL fixes almost no problem on which the base has an attractor.
starts_from: result-1dedfe / result-2c2cae (hard328 vote@4 only 179 against a 189 the sample-specific account needed, see r2-revise-2), result-5d032f (vote adds 8.2 to the base and 3.6 to RL) and result-9b6af3 (a random resample already solves 40 of the 65 'RL-only' problems)
differs_from: A revision of r2-revise-2, which said all of the base's residual errors are sample-specific commitment errors and was refuted by the hard328 vote count (claimed 189 [180, 198], measured 179). This revision splits errors into attractor and scattered errors and predicts that RL fails on exactly the attractor problems. r3-across-1 sorts problems by base p and not by the structure of wrong answers; m05 and m08 explain the item pattern by register prior and pretraining exposure.
first_test: day1_3 rows.jsonl (attempt 0) for both models, extracted_v3 and score_v3: for each problem, the base's modal wrong answer and its share among the base's wrong samples. (a) Of RL's wrong samples, the fraction equal to some base wrong answer on that problem, against a null that shuffles wrong answers between problems with the same gold type. (b) RL's fix rate (base vote wrong, RL vote right) on problems whose base modal wrong share is >= 0.5 vs < 0.5. Refuted if (a) is under 40 %, or if the fix rate in (b) is not at least 2x lower on attractor problems.

mechanism: Part of the cued base's accuracy is recall of solutions that sat in its pretraining text (short, low-entropy right answers), while RL learned procedures that carry over to problems the base never saw. So the RL-minus-cued-base gap is largest on problems published after the base's data cutoff, at matched difficulty.
starts_from: result-5e17a6 (base answers <= 2,000 tokens: 263, only 13 wrong), result-5de032 (hard328 gap by length quartile) and knowledge-42a54f (overlap of the harder set with RL prompts is by year)
differs_from: No graveyard theory uses data exposure. r3-across-1, r3-external-2 and r3-surprises-2 tie the hard-set gap to dose or long problems; m05 ties it to register prior, m07 to the structure of wrong answers. This one predicts a source-year effect that the others do not.
first_test: day1_hard328 answers.jsonl for base cue (e72c) and RL plain (86ef): map unique_id to source and year (AIME 2025 and HMMT Feb 2025 vs AIME 2022-24, AMC 23, OlympiadBench) and compute the paired RL-minus-base gap per group within RL-length quartiles (Mantel-Haenszel). On MATH-500, also compare sum_entropy_own/n_own (checks.json T1) of the base's short right answers against its long right answers. Refuted if the post-cutoff gap is under 1.5x the pre-cutoff gap with overlapping strata CIs, or if short right base answers are not lower in entropy per token.

mechanism: The math gain from Code-RL 3.1 is only a transferred ending policy: finish before the cap with one terminal delimited answer, then stop. 3.1's recipe teaches it by scoring truncated rollouts as failures and rewarding a final code block. It adds no correctness on problems the base already finishes cleanly, and Code 3.0 (truncations masked) lacks it even though its weight difference is larger.
starts_from: result-edceef (Code 3.1 cue 450 vs Code 3.0 cue 411, while 3.0 moved the weights further, 0.151 % vs 0.109 %), knowledge-9f8067 (Code 3.0 loops in 64 % of LiveCodeBench rollouts) and result-4b0d5f (Code-RL cue 3,336 tokens/problem, below the base's)
differs_from: r3-revise-1, r3-surprises-2 and r3-across-1 have Code share a domain-general deliberate-and-commit part (their Code 3.0 claims failed); r1-surprises-1 gives the termination component to 3.1 Math alone. This one says Code 3.1's whole gain is in base failures at the ending (cap hits, text continued past the answer, garbled final line). m03 predicts that Code and Math fix the same items, including clean wrong ones; the per-class split separates the two.
first_test: MATH-500: classify each problem by the base T1 answer (T1.jsonl): right; clean-finished-wrong (one final answer, EOS, no cap); ending-failure-wrong (cap_hit, or text after the last answer marker > 200 chars, or no extracted answer). Compute the fix rates of code_cue (0203), theta0.5_cue (683b) and random_cue (6429) per class. On hard328, compare Code a619 vs base e72c on base cap-hit vs finished-wrong problems. Refuted if Code's fix rate on clean-finished-wrong problems exceeds the random cell's by >= 10 points, or matches theta0.5's there.

mechanism: Early RL collapses entropy onto the base's own top paths and gives most of the gain on finished answers. Under T 0.6 / top-p 0.95 the lower-entropy policy loops more, not less. Only later, after truncated rollouts have been scored as negatives for many steps, are those loops removed. So cap hits at T 0.6 rise above the base's at steps 100-400 before falling by step 2,800.
starts_from: knowledge-9c5052 and knowledge-87618d (step 100 at the neuron noise floor, most decorrelation later), with knowledge-0b450e (step 100 and 400 rows exist, unscored) and knowledge-8a31ad (3.1 trains truncations as negatives)
differs_from: r3-all-1 has commit-and-box appear early and checking later, and says nothing about loops rising; r3-external-1 has 3.1's truncation negatives remove repetition basins without any early phase. r3-external-2 splits by sharpening and later expansion of coverage, measured on accuracy. This one makes a non-monotone prediction about cap hits over training: up first, then down.
first_test: Grade with v3 and compare r3 s0400_s0100-01 s0100/P_math500 and s0400/P_math500 (and s0400 F_math500) against base-01 P_math500 / F_math500 and s2800 P_math500 / F_math500, all at T 0.6 / top-p 0.95: cap-hit rate, rule-A loop rate, and accuracy on finished answers. Refuted if the cap-hit rate at step 100 or step 400 is below the base's (65 plain), or if accuracy on finished answers at step 400 is not at least halfway from base to step 2,800.

mechanism: The base, prompted for an 'Answer:' line, often does not emit EOS after it and goes on in pretraining mode (an invented follow-up problem, a variant, a reworking that changes the value). A last-marker grader then scores a later answer, so part of the cued base's residual deficit is a stopping-and-extraction artifact on answers whose first stated answer was right.
starts_from: knowledge-499152 (v3's only right-to-wrong flip comes from an invented COFFEE problem after the real answer), result-5e17a6 (8 of the 65 RL-only marked 'right answer in a rejected or garbled final line', 2 'reached gold then changed it') and result-96e819 (6 of the base's 7 review fixes are format repairs)
differs_from: r1-all-2 has a format switch in the weights; r2-surprises-1 used the v1/v2 miss counts as evidence of confusion. No graveyard entry has the gap living in text after the first answer. m12 is about grader recall on equivalent expressions, not about which answer gets extracted.
first_test: On T1.jsonl (base cue, T 1.0) and T2.jsonl (RL), re-extract the FIRST answer marker ('Answer:' line or \boxed) of each finished answer, regrade it with grader/rln4_grader_v3.py, and measure the text after it. Refuted if first-marker grading turns fewer than 10 of the 65 RL-only problems right, or if base wrong answers have no more post-answer text (> 300 chars) than base right answers.

mechanism: On the harder set, a rule-based grader's recall falls on expression-valued answers. RL learned to write the canonical simplified form its training verifier accepted, while the cued base writes equivalent but non-canonical forms. So part of the hard328 gap is a grader false-negative rate that is concentrated in the base's answers to non-integer problems.
starts_from: result-82b4dc / result-5de032 (hard328 gap 12.8 points, 33 of 49 RL-only being base finished-wrong answers) and knowledge-781efc / result-e78dfe (v3 lifted the base by 21 and RL by 5 over v1 on MATH-500: base answer forms are more varied)
differs_from: No graveyard theory puts any of the hard-set gap in the grader; result-0018d3 checked only false positives in v1/v3 disagreements, not false negatives on hard328. m11 is about which answer gets extracted on MATH-500; m12 is about equivalence recall by answer type on hard328.
first_test: day1_hard328 answers.jsonl for base cue (e72c) and RL plain (86ef): label gold as integer vs other (fraction, radical, expression, interval). For each base wrong answer with an extracted value, test numeric equivalence to gold (sympy evaluation, random substitution for variables) and count the false negatives per type and per model. Refuted if fewer than 4 base answers are recovered, or if the RL-only rate on non-integer problems is not at least 1.5x the rate on integer problems.
